heard: Dead stars are supposed to destroy worlds, not build new ones. Most astronomers believed a white dwarf, the dense remnant core of a dead star, was a planetary graveyard. But in 1999, the Hubble Space Telescope spotted 100 unidentified chemical signatures around the white dwarf HS2-09 plus 832. Recently, researcher Jamie Williams used an updated database to solve this 25-year-old cosmic cold case. The mystery signatures turned out to be niobium, a heavy metal forged only during stellar death throes. NASA's TESS telescope then detected a Jupiter-sized candidate planet orbiting the dead star every 4.4 days. The white dwarf's intense radiation is stripping this second-generation planet's atmosphere, raining those heavy metals back down. This cosmic recycling shows why dead stars are actually building new ones.
